query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Hf with an equivalent amount of Zr in the equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce the overall density while maintaining its high strength and stability from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and excellent mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace the heavy element Hf with a lighter, isostructural element (Zr) by adjusting the composition to remove Hf and increase Zr accordingly.
generation.conditions: The alloy is tested in the as-cast condition under tensile and compressive loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid-solution structure maintained through similar atomic radii and lattice parameters between Zr and the other constituent elements preserves the distortion-induced strengthening mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: Because Zr is substantially less dense than Hf yet exhibits comparable chemical and structural behavior, replacing Hf with Zr is expected to lower the alloy’s density while retaining the lattice distortions and phase stability that contribute to its high mechanical performance at both room and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in density relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr (ideally >5% decrease) with mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and creep resistance) that remain within 10% of the original values.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to as-cast high-entropy alloys tested under tensile/compressive conditions across a temperature range from room temperature to ~1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in density and the precise retention of mechanical properties are uncertain until experimentally validated; potential effects on microstructural stability due to the altered elemental balance may also need further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the standard as-cast HfMoTaTiZr composition and one with a modified composition where Hf is replaced by an equivalent atomic fraction of Zr. Perform density measurements and mechanical tests (tensile and compressive) at room temperature and ~1000 °C under identical processing conditions.
measurements: Creep resistance and yield strength at ~1000 °C
Microstructural analysis (e.g., XRD, SEM) to confirm phase stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Zr-substituted alloy exhibits either an insignificant reduction in density (less than ~5% reduction) or a degradation in mechanical performance (yield strength or creep resistance reduced by more than 10% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr) across the tested temperature range.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation

frame.system: The as‐cast equiatomic high‐entropy alloy HfMoTaTiZr, which is known for its high strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C but suffers from a high density (≈10.21 g/cm³).
frame.goal: Reduce the alloy’s density while retaining its excellent mechanical performance (strength and high‐temperature stability) across room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
frame.limitation: The alloy’s relatively high density limits its application in weight‐sensitive environments, despite its strong mechanical characteristics.
root_cause_cues: high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature
relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3
constraints: single intervention (i.e., one change to the alloy composition)
must not degrade mechanical properties at room temperature or at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C)
be applicable in the as‐cast state
frame.regime: Mechanical performance (e.g., tensile/compressive properties) measured at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to ~1000 °C under relevant loading conditions.
prior_attempts: While no explicit earlier attempts are cited, the literature on high‐entropy alloys often shows that altering element fractions via elemental substitution (for instance, replacing heavy elements with lighter, isostructural alternatives) can help reduce density. However, multiple interventions or compromises in the phase stability/strength have been noted in past efforts, which this single‐intervention strategy aims to avoid.
frame.understanding: Proposed Intervention and Mechanism: Replace the heavy element Hf with a lighter but similar element (for example, by fully or partially substituting Hf with additional Zr) because Hf (density ~13.3 g/cm³) and Zr (density ~6.5 g/cm³) have similar chemical and atomic size characteristics. This substitution should lower the overall alloy density while maintaining the lattice distortion and solid‐solution strengthening mechanisms that underpin the excellent mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures. The expected directional change is a significant decrease in density without a detrimental impact (i.e., less than a nominal loss, such as within 5–10% of yield strength or creep resistance) on strength and high‐temperature performance. The applicable testing boundaries include mechanical testing from room temperature to ~1000 °C under representative tensile and compressive loads. Prior supporting evidence is found in studies on high‐entropy and refractory alloys where isovalent substitutions (e.g., Hf/Zr comparisons) preserved phase stability and strength while reducing density. Experimental validation would involve casting a modified alloy (e.g., with Hf replaced by Zr to form a Zr-rich variant such as MoTaTiZr + extra Zr), then measuring its density and mechanical properties across the temperature range. The rejection criterion would be if the modified alloy exhibits mechanical properties (at room temperature and ~1000 °C) that are significantly inferior (for example, more than a 10% drop in yield stress or creep resistance) compared to the standard as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr.
